title: Unlearning Is an Important Part of Learning
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article treats unlearning — deliberately replacing outdated beliefs, opinions, and habits — as a distinct and underrated leadership skill, separate from simply forgetting. The hardest part, it argues, is identification: even self-aware leaders struggle to see what needs to be unlearned on their own, and often rely on a telltale pattern of repeated, consistent poor outcomes tied to the same habit or belief. It walks through the process end-to-end: recognizing the pattern, gathering evidence for a better alternative before committing to it, and then reinforcing the new approach through conscious, repeated practice. The piece closes by noting third parties like executive coaches play an outsized role, since they can spot the blind spot a leader can't see in themselves and hold them accountable for actually changing.
points: Unlearning is distinguished explicitly from forgetting — it's about reevaluating and replacing, not erasing.
The hardest part of unlearning is identification, since even highly self-aware leaders rarely spot on their own what needs to go.
A repeated pattern of poor outcomes tied to the same habit, belief, or approach is the key diagnostic signal to watch for.
Third parties like executive coaches play an outsized role, both in spotting blind spots and in holding leaders accountable through the change.
quotes: Letting go of outdated beliefs, inaccurate opinions, and unproductive habits makes room for new ideas and practices.
Unlearning isn’t about forgetting. It is about reevaluating and replacing.
Identifying what needs to be unlearned is the biggest challenge. Even highly self-aware leaders are unlikely to know what they need to unlearn.
That’s why third parties, such as executive coaches and mentors, can play such a pivotal role in the process.
The best leaders learn, unlearn, and relearn. They know self-improvement and quality decision-making depend on it.
